transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-22 15:00 PST | Duration 48m | Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Raman, Luis Ortega (Redwood); Marcus Holt, Sofia Perez, Anita Chow (Tildex)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick check — can we do audio checks?
[00:08] Marcus Holt: yup good here, Sofia good, Anita good.
[00:12] Jordan: awesome so this is the weekly econ sync for the pilot, main agenda: tokens per dollar, caching numbers, and batching tradeoffs. Priya will walk through the recent telemetry.
[00:26] Priya Raman: cool hi all, i pulled the last 72 hours of traffic from the Dedicated pilot — note some of the labels got munged in export so there might be small mismatches. overall average tokens/sec per GPU is about 1,820 tokens/sec under the mixed workload, but cost per token varies by model variant and quantization.
[00:45] Anita Chow: when you say mixed workload, is that 50/50 short prompts and long completions?
[00:51] Priya: roughly yes — 60% short (<=64 tokens) and 40% long (>256). Short prompts push latency sensitive paths so batching benefits are limited.
[01:05] Luis Ortega: a quick caveat — our telemetry tags the variant as "rwd-v1-8k-int8" in some rows and the exporter turned that into rwd-v1-eight-k-int. so numbers are approximate.
[01:18] Marcus: ok fair. can you give the tokens per dollar with and without caching? that's the big one for us.
[01:24] Priya: sure. baseline (no cache) tokens/$ for the current config is about 3,200 tokens per dollar. with prefix caching enabled we measured a median uplift to ~5,100 tokens/$, so roughly 60% improvement. KV cache hits only applied for 18% of requests because your memoization pattern is not always prefix-stable.
[01:42] Sofia: 18% KV hit — that seems lower than we expected, we thought our FAQ responses would hit more. Are we sure the prefix matching logic wasn't too strict?
[01:50] Priya: yeah that's likely — the cache keying used exact token-level prefix match in this run. we can relax to semantic-prefix or lower the ngram threshold, which should bump hit rates. tradeoff is more cache pollution and slightly higher miss latency sometimes.
[02:05] Jordan: quick interjection — from a unit economics angle, even small increases in hit-rate matter a lot because cached responses bypass decoding on the GPU, so token cost goes to near-zero for those.
[02:20] Anita: can you quantify how much tail-latency changes with larger batch sizes? our SLO is 150ms p95 for short prompts.
[02:29] Priya: we ran two configs: batch window 10ms vs 50ms. With 10ms window p95 for short prompts was 130ms, tokens/sec lower. With 50ms batching we saw tokens/sec improve by ~22% but p95 climbed to ~210ms, so that violates your 150ms SLO.
[02:49] Marcus: so we can't just crank batching to get cheaper tokens, because product UX would be impacted.
[02:55] Luis: exactly. There's also continuous batching heuristics — dynamic window that grows under low QPS and shrinks under high QPS. That helps average throughput without blowing p95 as much.
[03:07] Jordan: we should probably add that as a config in the pilot: dynamic batching with a hard cap on window to keep p95 under 150ms.
[03:15] Sofia: can you do that and re-run the benchmark? we want to see net tokens/$ with dynamic batching + relaxed prefix cache.
[03:23] Priya: yes, we can schedule that. quick note on quantization: using int8 variants we shave ~18% off per-token GPU cost but see subtle quality diffs on long-form answers. your eval set had a few regressions in factuality which you flagged.
[03:41] Anita: yeah product cares about hallucinations, especially in the longer answers. are those regressions in open-qa or in step-by-step?
[03:47] Priya: mostly long procedural answers — sometimes the int8 model elides details. we can try mixed strategy: int8 for short prompts, fp16 for long ones — routing based on prompt length.
[03:58] Marcus: that sounds promising. how much complexity does routing add operationally?
[04:03] Luis: minimal — it's a policy layer in the router. it's a small config: if prompt_tokens > 200 route to fp16 model family. But it does increase cost buckets to track.
[04:13] Jordan: ok to recap: dynamic batching + relaxed prefix cache + routing by prompt length to model family. Priya will run benchmark. Jordan will update cost spreadsheet.
[04:23] Sofia: a question on cache warm-up — do you pre-populate the prefix cache during rollout?
[04:28] Priya: we can seed the cache with the top 1k queries from logs. that improves early hit-rate and reduces noisy warm-up effects. For the pilot we seeded with last week's top 500 queries; we can increase to 1k.
[04:40] Anita: sounds good. also can you share the cache hit distribution? median and tail?
[04:46] Priya: median hit rate for this run was 18% as mentioned; 90th percentile was 42% because a small set of templates hit very frequently. we can add TTLs to evict stale entries and improve overall efficacy.
[05:00] Marcus: any thoughts on routing to cheaper regions or model variants when load spikes? cost vs latency tradeoff there.
[05:07] Jordan: we discussed smart routing in the deck — you can set policies to route non-critical requests to lower-cost variants or different regions. Important to be careful with data residency.
[05:18] Sofia: yes we need to keep EU data in EU region; some traffic is EU. how did region-specific numbers look?
[05:24] Priya: EU nodes had slightly higher per-token cost due to smaller instance types in that region — tokens/$ about 10% worse than US-west in this pilot. We can estimate that in the updated sheet.
[05:35] Luis: also, if you want to reduce cost without touching model quality, consider KV prefix compression on the key, which reduces memory footprint and can increase effective cache size. small wins add up.
[05:47] Marcus: do you have concrete numbers on memory improvement?
[05:50] Luis: roughly 30% smaller keys when we apply simple hashing + compression, which increases hitable entries by similar factor depending on working set.
[05:58] Anita: on the topic of billing, how will Redwood show these savings? per-token billing or a combined line item for cache hits?
[06:06] Jordan: currently billing is per-token normalized plus separate line items for Dedicated capacity. Cache savings show up as lower effective tokens consumed. We can provide a modeled tokens/sec/$ column that projects net unit economics with cache and batching assumptions; that's what we'll add to the spreadsheet.
[06:20] Sofia: perfect. can you walk through one worked example? like 1M monthly queries with current profile.
[06:26] Priya: sure — short version: baseline cost for 1M queries was $X (we used $0.30 per 1M tokens as a placeholder in the sheet), with current traffic mix the model yields ~3,200 tokens/$ so cost was ~ $312/month. With prefix caching uplift and dynamic batching the projected tokens/$ jumps to 5,000 so cost drops to ~$200/month. these are illustrative; final numbers in spreadsheet.
[06:52] Marcus: I see. small clarifying note: in your sheet please show assumptions (tokenization, average tokens per request for short and long).
[06:58] Jordan: will do.
[07:01] Anita: any issues with security/compliance for caching? e.g., customer PII accidentally cached?
[07:07] Priya: we flagged that earlier — by default we recommend filtering or hashing sensitive fields before caching and using the private deployment KMS to encrypt the cache store. Also set explicit TTLs and audit logs.
[07:18] Marcus: okay will take that back to compliance team.
[07:22] Sofia: quick question — you mentioned earlier some transcription or labeling glitches in the exporter. can we get raw logs for the benchmark run?
[07:28] Priya: yes we'll upload the raw logs and a sanitized trace to the shared drive. link in follow-up.
[07:34] Jordan: good, moving on — next, planned benchmark: dynamic batching enabled, prefix-caching with relaxed ngram threshold, seed top-1k queries, run for 4 hours during controlled load window. Priya to capture p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec and cache hit distribution.
[07:50] Marcus: timeline?
[07:52] Priya: earliest we can do it is Friday (2026-07-24) evening PST, or Monday. Marcus: Friday works for us.
[07:59] Jordan: great. then we'll reconvene next week with results. Anything else?
[08:04] Anita: one last thing — can Redwood provide a short note on how dynamic batching reacts to bursty traffic? we need to explain it to our infra team.
[08:12] Luis: yes we'll prepare a 1-page doc that explains heuristics: min/max window, backpressure signal, and how it interacts with KV cache.
[08:20] Jordan: excellent. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and scheduling.
[08:25] (crosstalk) Sofia: thanks all.
[48:00] Meeting end.

Notes: shared artifacts referenced — cost_model_v2.xlsx (internal link), pilot_benchmark_logs_20260722.tar (pending upload), Redwood dynamic-batching-one-pager (to be attached). Some transcriptions may have label errors (rwd-v1-8k-int8 appears as rwd-v1-eight-k-int).
